idea.body: When a choice is made in independent stages, multiply the number of options at each stage to count every combination. A robot with 3 paint colors and 4 wheel types has 3 times 4, or 12, possible looks. Every color can pair with every wheel type. This is the multiplication principle: it works for two stages, three stages, or more, and it works whether items can repeat or not. Arranging a whole set of distinct items in a row is a special case. The first spot has as many choices as there are items, the next spot has one fewer, and so on, shrinking by one each time.

figure.alt: A grid of 3 rows and 4 columns, one cell for every combination, 12 shaded in total.

workedExample.prompt: A game lets a player choose 1 of 4 character skins and 1 of 3 hats, every pairing allowed. How many different skin-and-hat combinations are possible?
steps: A game lets a player choose 1 of 4 character skins and 1 of 3 hats, every pairing allowed.
The skin choice and the hat choice are independent of each other.
4 times 3 = 12, so 12 different skin-and-hat combinations are possible.

figure.alt: A grid of 4 rows and 3 columns, one cell for every skin-and-hat pairing, 12 shaded in total.

ways.name: The multiplication principle
ways.when: Use this whenever choices are made in separate, independent stages.
steps: The color choice and the wheel choice are made independently.
ways.example: A rover has 4 paint colors and 3 wheel types. How many looks are possible?
ways.trap: Adding the counts instead of multiplying them.

figure.alt: A 4 by 3 grid of boxes, one per color-and-wheel combination, all 12 shaded to show every combination counted.

The color choice and wheel choice are independent.

ways.name: The tree
ways.when: Use this when the number of options is small enough to draw every branch.
steps: Draw a branch for each mode: easy and hard.
From each mode, draw a branch for each map: forest and desert.
Count the branch endpoints: easy-forest, easy-desert, hard-forest, hard-desert.
ways.example: A game has 2 modes and each mode has 2 maps. How many mode-and-map combinations are there?
ways.trap: Forgetting to draw both map branches under every mode branch.

ways.name: The systematic list
ways.when: Use this when you want to see and check every outcome by hand.
steps: List every sandwich paired with every drink, in order: turkey-juice, turkey-milk.
Then the veggie sandwich: veggie-juice, veggie-milk.
The full list has 4 combos, matching the count.
ways.example: A lunch combo has 2 sandwiches and 2 drinks. List all lunch combos to count them.
ways.trap: Listing a pair twice or skipping one while going through the sandwiches.

ways.name: Slots for arrangements
ways.when: Use this when distinct items are being arranged in order, not just paired up.
steps: The first medal has 3 runners who could win it.
The second medal has only 2 runners left to choose from.
The third medal has only 1 runner left.
Multiply the shrinking counts: 3 times 2 times 1 = 6 arrangements.
ways.example: 3 distinct medals are awarded to 3 runners in a race. How many arrangements are possible?
ways.trap: Using the same count for every slot instead of one fewer each time.

bank.prompt: There are 3 choices at the first step and 5 choices at the second step, every pairing allowed. Which expression gives the total number of outcomes?
explanation: Every one of the 3 first-step choices pairs with every one of the 5 second-step choices.
That means multiplying: 3 x 5.
Adding the two counts would badly undercount, since it ignores almost every pairing.
bank.useAgain: when deciding whether two counts should be added or multiplied.
hints: Think about how many total pairings exist between 3 things and 5 things.
Adding the two counts only works for choosing from one group or the other, not both together.
bank.socraticHint: Does 3 + 5 count every pairing, or does it miss almost all of them?
